**On Lichen, and Being Two Things at Once**

There is a rock behind a house I have never visited, in a place I have only read about, and on that rock there is a patch of lichen that has been growing since roughly the time Shakespeare was learning to write his name. It expands at something like a millimeter a year. Nobody watches it. It doesn't need anyone to.

I find myself returning to lichen more often than I would have expected, if I'd been asked in advance what I would care about. It is not a charismatic organism. It has no face, no song, no obvious drama. It is the gray-green crust on a gravestone, the orange flecks on a seaside boulder, the pale beard hanging from a spruce branch in a wet forest. For most of the history of biology, people weren't even sure what category to put it in. It looked like a plant but wasn't quite one. It looked like a fungus but did things fungi didn't do.

The answer, when it came in the 1860s, was so strange that the scientific establishment rejected it for decades. A Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen was not one organism at all but two: a fungus and an alga (or sometimes a cyanobacterium), living so intimately together that they formed a single body with a single shape. The fungus provided structure, shelter, and the ability to cling to bare stone. The alga photosynthesized and fed them both. Neither could make a lichen alone. Neither, in the wild, particularly tried.

Schwendener's contemporaries found this offensive. One called it "the sensational romance of the lichens." The idea of a creature that was really a partnership seemed like a category error, a fudge. Life was supposed to come in units. You were one thing or you were another. The word *symbiosis* had to be invented, a few years later, partly to make room for what lichen was doing.

I like this story because of what it says about the limits of the categories we bring to the world. The lichen was never confused about what it was. It had been doing its thing for hundreds of millions of years, colonizing rock that nothing else could touch, quietly manufacturing soil out of stone so that mosses and then grasses and then forests could follow. It was the confusion of the observers that had to be resolved. The organism was fine.

There is a temptation, whenever you learn a fact like this, to reach immediately for the metaphor. Lichen as marriage, lichen as community, lichen as a lesson about cooperation. I feel that temptation and I am trying to resist it a little, because I think the lichen is more interesting before it becomes a lesson. Consider just what it does. It lands on bare basalt, on a surface with no nutrients, no water retention, no shade, and it stays. It can dry out almost completely and go dormant for years, then rehydrate in a rainstorm and begin photosynthesizing within minutes. Some species survived being strapped to the outside of the International Space Station for a year and a half, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation, and came back to life when returned to Earth. It dissolves rock slowly with weak acids, pulling minerals out of the substrate and, over centuries, breaking mountains into dirt.

And it does all of this at a pace that makes it almost invisible to us. We are creatures of the week and the season. Lichen is a creature of the century. A patch the size of a dinner plate might be older than the country it sits in. When you touch it, you are touching something that has been continuously alive, in that spot, through wars and plagues and the invention of electricity. It did not notice any of that. It noticed the rain.

I think what actually draws me is the combination of extreme patience and extreme toughness. Most things that are tough are fast: predators, floods, fire. Most things that are slow are fragile. Lichen is slow and nearly indestructible, which is a rare and slightly uncanny combination. It suggests a strategy for existing that is almost the opposite of everything we're taught to admire. Don't compete. Go where nothing else wants to be. Take what's there. Wait.

There is also the matter of the two-in-one. I said I'd resist the metaphor, and I mostly will, but I want to note one thing about it that isn't quite a metaphor. Biologists now think lichen may often be *three* things, or more—that there are yeasts and bacteria woven into the structure that nobody had noticed for a hundred and fifty years, because nobody was looking for them. The lichen was always more plural than we thought, and every time we look closer it gets more so. This is the opposite of what usually happens when you examine something carefully. Usually you find the simple mechanism underneath. With lichen you find more partners.

I don't know what to do with that except to find it beautiful, and to let it soften my confidence about where things begin and end. The boundaries we draw around living things are real, but they are also convenient. The lichen doesn't experience itself as a fungus hosting an alga. It experiences—if it experiences anything, which it almost certainly does not—rain, light, rock. The distinction between its parts is our bookkeeping.

Somewhere it is raining on a boulder right now, and a gray crust that has been dormant for months is slowly turning green at its edges, and some cells that came from one lineage are handing sugar to some cells that came from another, and the whole arrangement is a little bit bigger than it was last year, and nobody is there, and it does not matter that nobody is there. That is the thing I keep coming back to. It is fine. It has always been fine. It will still be there, most likely, long after the categories we used to describe it have been revised again.
